sources.title: AWARE-AWAreness during REsuscitation-a prospective study
sources.study_design: four-year multicentre prospective observational study with staged survivor interviews and feasibility testing of objective visual/auditory verification
limitations: Only a small survivor subset of all cardiac-arrest events could be interviewed.
Retrospective verbal report cannot by itself establish the exact neurophysiological timing of an experience.
The study's objective-target design produced very limited opportunities for target verification.
The study concerns cardiac arrest and resuscitation, not irreversible biological death.

sources.title: AWAreness during REsuscitation - II: A multi-center study of consciousness and awareness in cardiac arrest
sources.study_design: multicentre prospective in-hospital cardiac-arrest study using survivor interviews plus audiovisual testing, EEG and cerebral oximetry in instrumented cases
limitations: Interview data came from a small subset of the enrolled cardiac-arrest population.
Physiological monitoring was not complete or continuous for every arrest and every interval.
Recall after recovery does not uniquely determine when the remembered experience occurred.
Cardiac arrest under attempted resuscitation is not equivalent to irreversible biological death.

sources.title: Critical dynamics in spontaneous EEG predict anesthetic-induced loss of consciousness and perturbational complexity
sources.study_design: analysis of EEG and perturbational-complexity data from 15 healthy adults exposed to propofol, xenon or ketamine anesthesia
limitations: Small sample with five participants per anesthetic group.
Consciousness classification depended partly on post-recovery reports of subjective experience.
Anesthetic perturbation is a model of altered consciousness, not a test of post-mortem consciousness.
Associations between EEG criticality measures and consciousness do not establish metaphysical necessity or sufficiency.

claims.text: In AWARE 2014, 140 survivors completed stage-1 interviews after 2,060 cardiac-arrest events, and 101 completed stage-2 interviews.
provenance: peer-reviewed article abstract and bibliographic record
limitations: These denominators constrain generalisation from interviewed survivors to all cardiac-arrest events.
claims.uncertainty: No inference about post-mortem survival follows from these denominators alone.

claims.text: AWARE 2014 reported that 2% of interviewed participants described explicit recall of seeing or hearing events related to resuscitation, with one case reported as containing verifiable event details.
limitations: Reported recall is not equivalent to proof that experience occurred during a period of absent brain function.
Objective visual-target verification was extremely limited.
claims.uncertainty: The exact timing and neurophysiological substrate of the reported experience remain uncertain.

claims.text: AWARE II enrolled 567 in-hospital cardiac arrests; 53 people survived and 28 survivors were interviewed.
provenance: peer-reviewed article and indexed bibliographic record
limitations: The interview sample was a small survivor subset of the enrolled population.
claims.uncertainty: The survivor and interview selection process limits population-wide inference.

claims.text: In a 15-participant anesthetic dataset, propofol and xenon conditions classified as unconscious differed in EEG criticality measures from wakefulness, while ketamine produced behavioral unresponsiveness with reported conscious dream-like experience and more wakefulness-like critical dynamics.
limitations: Five participants were studied per anesthetic group.
The work tests pharmacologically altered consciousness, not biological death.
claims.uncertainty: The findings support brain-state/conscious-state relationships under the tested conditions but do not determine whether consciousness could ever continue outside those conditions.

claims.text: The neural-correlates research programme provides a disciplined framework for identifying neural mechanisms associated with conscious experience while distinguishing correlates, enabling conditions and report-related activity.
limitations: A neural correlate is not automatically a complete causal or ontological explanation of consciousness.
claims.uncertainty: The relationship between neural correlates and the ultimate metaphysics of consciousness remains unresolved.

batch_conclusion.statement: Batch 1 establishes reproducible observations about reported experiences around resuscitation and experimentally measurable brain-state/conscious-state relationships. These observations constrain competing models but do not establish either post-mortem continuity or its impossibility.
